note: _una hora facere_ – to work for one hour (ablative). One would expect _laborare_ instead of _facere_. The verb _facere_ does not seem to have this precise meaning elsewhere; it echoes the underlying Greek ποιεῖν, which in Ruth 2:19 (Septuagint) also means “to work” in an agricultural context. The underlying Greek μίαν ὥραν ἐποίησαν actually means “they have spent one hour” which, in Latin, would be _unam horam fecerunt_; compare Seneca: _Letters_ 66,4: _quamvis autem paucissimos una fecerimus dies_ – while we were together only for a few days).

_principes gentium dominantur eorum_ – the princes of the Gentiles control them. The verb _dominari_, to control (verbum deponens), is followed by genitive; it should be earum (fem.) because _gens_ is a feminine word. Interestingly, or by oversight, NVg has kept _eorum_.
